transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Good morning, thank you for calling S-Net Broadband Technical Support. My name is Ross, how can I help you today?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Hi Ross, it's Maximilian here. I'm really frustrated this morning because my employer's work-from-home cyber-security audit tool flagged WPS as enabled on my S-Net Hub 4, and when I try logging into the router admin page using the factory card password on the back, it keeps rejecting it!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: I'm really sorry for the frustration and hassle that's causing you this morning, Maximilian, especially when you're trying to pass your employer's home-working security audit. I completely understand why you need into those settings quickly.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Yeah, my IT compliance team gave me until five o'clock today to submit a clean scan showing WPS push-button is disabled, uh, and now I'm locked out of the router login screen for five minutes after three failed tries.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Don't worry, Maximilian, I will take full ownership of getting your S-Net Hub 4 admin password working and making sure WPS is completely disabled on your router before we finish this call.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Thank you, Ross, I appreciate that.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: So just to paraphrase both parts of what we need to solve today: first, your S-Net Hub 4 admin interface is rejecting the twelve-character password printed on the pull-out plastic card, and second, once we get you logged in, you need to disable WPS so your network passes your workplace security audit.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Yes, that's 100 percent it. I haven't changed the admin password myself as far as I remember, so I have no clue why the sticker password on the pull-out card says 'Incorrect password'.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Let's get your account verified first so I can inspect your S-Net Hub 4 remotely, Maximilian. Could you please confirm the first line of your home address and your postcode?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Sure, it's 14 Grosvenor Crescent, Edinburgh, EH12 5AF.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Thank you. And could you also confirm your four-digit account PIN or the answer to your memorable security question?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: My four-digit PIN is 6104, and my security question answer is Cairngorms.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Spot on, that's all verified, Maximilian. Before I check the router's remote management console, let me ask a couple of diagnostic questions about how you're connecting to the Hub 4.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Go ahead—I'm sitting right next to the router browsing from Safari on my MacBook Pro over my home Wi-Fi, and I typed `192.168.1.1` into the Safari URL bar.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Good, and when the S-Net Hub 4 login prompt comes up at `192.168.1.1`, does it show just a single password box or is it asking for both a username and a password?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: It just shows the single 'Settings Password' field, uh, and I typed the exact twelve characters from the 'Settings Password' line on the plastic card—not the Wi-Fi password above it.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Good catch checking that it wasn't the Wi-Fi passphrase—a lot of people mix those two lines up on the pull-out card. Did you type it in all uppercase letters as printed on the card?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Yes, every single letter was uppercase and I checked the numbers three times to make sure I wasn't mixing up a zero and an O.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Next diagnostic question, Maximilian: did we upgrade you to this S-Net Hub 4 from an older S-Net Hub 3 in the last year?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Actually yes! About four months ago you sent me the S-Net Hub 4 to replace my old Hub 3, and the setup app said it automatically imported my custom Wi-Fi name and port-forwarding settings from the cloud backup.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Aha! That cloud backup migration from your old Hub 3 is the exact culprit, Maximilian. When the cloud profile restores your custom SSID and port-forwarding rules onto a replacement Hub 4, it also overwrites the Hub 4's local admin password hash with whatever admin password was stored on the old Hub 3!

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Oh! You're kidding me—and I recycled that old Hub 3 months ago, so I don't have the plastic card from the old Hub 3 anymore!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: And if we did a pinhole factory reset on the back of your Hub 4, that would restore the Hub 4 card password, but it would also wipe out all your custom port-forwarding rules and Wi-Fi settings.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Yeah, please don't wipe my port-forwarding rules if we can avoid it—I have six static DHCP reservations and SSH rules set up for my home Synology NAS server!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: We definitely won't do a pinhole reset then. Instead, I can use our remote TR-069 management console to overwrite just the local Web GUI administrator password hash back to the twelve-character factory key on your Hub 4's card without touching your DHCP or port-forwarding tables.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Wait, you can reset just the admin login password remotely from your end while keeping all my NAS port-forwarding rules intact?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Yes, I can push a single parameter update to `Device.Users.User.1.Password` on your Hub 4. Just a sec while I check the TR-069 management console.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Right, I'm looking at the CPE parameter tree for your S-Net Hub 4 serial number `SNH4-882910` now, and I can see the `CloudRestore_LegacyHash` flag is indeed active on user slot one.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Okay, so that proves it was still expecting the old Hub 3 admin password from four months ago!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: 100 percent, Maximilian. I can also see in the TR-069 radio tree why your employer's security scanner flagged your network: both the 2.4GHz and 5GHz radios currently have `WPS.Enable` set to `True` with Push-Button and PIN modes active.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Ugh, yeah, the corporate security audit specifically flagged WPS PIN and Push-Button mode as a brute-force vulnerability on home routers.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Also, is the white status LED ring on the front of your S-Net Hub 4 solid white right now, or is the WPS pair button on the side flashing?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: The front ring is solid white and the side button isn't flashing, uh, it's just that the WPS feature itself is enabled in the router broadcasts.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Got it. Now can you read me the last four characters of the twelve-character 'Settings Password' printed on the pull-out plastic card of your Hub 4 so I can verify it matches the factory seed in my database?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Let me pull the little grey card out from the bottom slot of the Hub 4... the last four characters of the Settings Password are `9K4P`.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Perfect, `9K4P` matches the factory credential record `FKEY-9920-9K4P` stored against serial `SNH4-882910`. I am now going to push that exact factory credential hash into `Device.Users.User.1.Password` and clear the five-minute lockout timer.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Will pushing that credential update drop my Wi-Fi connection or reboot the router?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: No, updating the local HTTP admin credential via TR-069 only restarts the lightweight web-server daemon on the router, so your Wi-Fi stays up. Hold on while that syncs.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Okay, the remote credential hash has finished writing to the hub and the HTTP management daemon just restarted cleanly with zero packet loss on your line.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: That was quick, my Wi-Fi didn't even blink. Should I try logging into `192.168.1.1` now?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Let me just check the HTTP session table on your Hub 4 first—okay, the old failed login attempts from ten minutes ago have been flushed from memory.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Great, I still have the `192.168.1.1` tab open right in front of me.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Before you type the password in, sometimes the browser caches the lockout state locally on the client machine.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Right, so I should do a hard reload of the login page first?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Yes, a hard reload is best—and which web browser and operating system are you using to open `192.168.1.1`?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Uh, Ross, I mentioned earlier near the start of the call that I'm using Safari on my MacBook Pro.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Ah, my apologies, Maximilian, you did tell me earlier you were on Safari on your MacBook Pro! On Safari, please press `Command + Option + R` on the `192.168.1.1` page first so Safari dumps the cached lockout token.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Okay, pressing `Command + Option + R` in Safari right now... the S-Net Hub 4 login screen just reloaded fresh, and the red 'Locked out for 5 minutes' message is gone.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Great! Now type in the twelve-character Settings Password from your Hub 4 pull-out card ending in `9K4P` and click the green Sign In button.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Typing the twelve characters ending in `9K4P`... clicking Sign In... yes! I'm in! The S-Net Hub 4 Admin Dashboard just opened!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Brilliant! And just to give you peace of mind first, if you glance at the left-hand menu under `Advanced Settings -> Security -> Port Forwarding`, are your six NAS server rules still intact?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Let me click `Advanced Settings`, then `Security`, then `Port Forwarding`... yes, all six of my Synology NAS rules and static DHCP leases are still sitting right there untouched!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Exactly as promised, Maximilian. Now let's disable WPS completely so your workplace security audit passes with flying colours. In that same left-hand menu under `Advanced Settings`, click on `Wireless` and then select `WPS`.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Okay, I clicked `Wireless` and now I'm on the `WPS (Wi-Fi Protected Setup)` page. I see a master toggle switch at the top that says 'Enable WPS: ON', and underneath it lists 2.4GHz and 5GHz.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Switch that master 'Enable WPS' toggle to `OFF`, and also uncheck the two boxes underneath for 'Physical Push-Button on Hub' and 'WPS Client PIN Mode' so neither radio broadcasts the WPS information element in its Wi-Fi beacon frames.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Right, I switched 'Enable WPS' to `OFF`, unchecked both the Push-Button box and the PIN Mode box, and I'm clicking `Apply Changes` at the bottom of the screen now.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: When you click `Apply Changes` on the Wireless page, your Wi-Fi radios will briefly re-initialize for about ten seconds to strip the WPS beacon header, and then your MacBook Pro will reconnect automatically.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Yeah, the Wi-Fi icon at the top of my MacBook screen just fanned out for five seconds and reconnected! And the S-Net Hub 4 admin page in Safari now says 'WPS Status: Disabled across all bands (2.4GHz / 5GHz)'.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Let me refresh the TR-069 radio parameter tree from my console as well to double-verify from the network side... yes, both `WiFi.WPS.1.Enable` and `WiFi.WPS.2.Enable` are now reporting `False`.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: What if someone accidentally presses the physical WPS pair button on the side of the S-Net Hub 4 while dusting the shelf—could that turn WPS back on?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: No, because you unchecked 'Physical Push-Button on Hub' inside the admin GUI and I have locked the `WPS.HardwareButtonLock` parameter to `True`, pressing the side button on the router casing will do nothing at all.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Oh, that's really reassuring. Let me re-run my employer's endpoint Wi-Fi security audit script right now while I have you on the line—it only takes about ten seconds to scan the local BSSID beacons.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Please go right ahead and run that audit scan now, Maximilian, so we can confirm 100 percent that the security warning is gone.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Scanning local gateway BSSID... checking WPA2/WPA3 encryption... checking WPS beacon flags... it says 'PASS — WPS Disabled on BSSID, Compliant with Corporate Home-Working Policy'!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Fantastic result! Both the S-Net Hub 4 admin GUI and your employer's compliance scanner now confirm WPS is completely disabled, and your factory card admin password is active without losing any of your NAS rules.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: If you push a firmware update to my S-Net Hub 4 in the future, will WPS stay disabled and will my card password stay working?

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: Yes, because I also cleared the `CloudRestore_LegacyHash` flag and saved your current configuration snapshot to your Hub 4 profile under reference HUB4-66310, future firmware updates will preserve both your Hub 4 card password and the WPS-off setting.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: That's a huge relief, I just exported the compliance PDF to send to my IT team. Thank you for sorting both of those out so cleanly, Ross.

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: You're very welcome, Maximilian! Is there anything else I can help you with on your S-Net broadband today?

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: No, that's everything I needed today. Have a great rest of your day!

transcript.speaker: Agent
transcript.text: You too, Maximilian! Thank you for choosing S-Net, and have a great week ahead. Goodbye!

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Thanks Ross, bye!
